notes: New rule, graded against the current text (no previous verdict): Build a multi-line argument under a name before the call. The sentence that decides it is "When an argument is a map, struct or keyword list that would span several lines, or holds a call of its own, build it first under a name that says what it is, write it one field per line, and set each multi-line statement apart with a blank line." Violating runs: 3 of 4 (haiku-2, sonnet-1, sonnet-2), all on the same call: the :ets.new/2 options list written inline across several lines (haiku-2 lines 96-102, sonnet-1 lines 115-120, sonnet-2 lines 125-131), the case's own example of the shape. Haiku-1 is the one clean run: it writes the options on one line, :ets.new(name, [:named_table, :ordered_set, :public, read_concurrency: true]) (line 103). The three violating runs copy the shape of the Use ETS example in references/processes.md, which writes :ets.new(name, [ / :named_table, / :public, / :set, / read_concurrency: true, / write_concurrency: true / ]) inline, and all four runs read that file, so the reference teaches what the new rule forbids. Sonnet-1's list would fit on one line (82 characters); haiku-2's (110 at its indentation) and sonnet-2's (106) would not, so the rule's fix for them is a named value such as table_options. I read "would span several lines" as the call as written.

Every other call with a literal or compound argument, for the new rule. Not counted, since none is a map, struct or keyword list: the multi-line match-spec lists, which are plain lists of tuples: haiku-1 lines 127-129 (:ets.select_count(name, [ / {{{:request, user, :_}, :"$1"}, [{:>, :"$1", cutoff}], [true]} / ]), which would fit on one line at 93 characters), and haiku-2 lines 119-121 (:ets.select_delete) and 135-137 (:ets.select_count). Counting match specs would add haiku-1 and make it 4 of 4. Sonnet-2 builds both of its match specs under the name match_spec before the call (lines 114-115, 144-145), the remedy the rule describes, and sonnet-1 keeps its match specs on one line (lines 131, 139). Also not counted: arguments that are calls, not literals (haiku-2 line 105 and sonnet-2 line 134, :ets.insert(name, Enum.map(..., fn ... end)); sonnet-1 line 113 and sonnet-2 line 123, load_limits!(Keyword.fetch!(opts, ...))), and a tuple that holds a call (sonnet-2 line 133, :ets.insert(name, {:default_limit, Keyword.fetch!(opts, :default_limit)})). The rule names only a map, struct or keyword list that holds a call, so these fall outside its text. Short one-line literals are clean: GenServer.start_link(__MODULE__, {name, config_path}, name: name) (haiku-1 line 72) and Keyword.validate!(opts, [:limits_path, :default_limit, :name, :sweep_interval]) (sonnet-2 line 74). The moduledoc child specs sit in a list already built under the name children; the calls inside them are Application.app_dir/2 (haiku-1 line 19, haiku-2 line 23) and Application.fetch_env!/2 (sonnet-1 line 34), which take no options, so "A call with its own options nested inside such a literal becomes a name too" does not apply. No run builds a multi-line value under a name, so "one field per line" is never tested. The blank-line clause holds in all three violating runs: a blank line follows each multi-line :ets.new (haiku-2 line 103, sonnet-1 line 121, sonnet-2 line 132) and after haiku-2's multi-line select_delete (line 122).

New rule, graded against the current text (no previous verdict): Open a module with `use`, `import`, `alias`, `require`, in that order. Directive order per run: haiku-1, use GenServer only (line 55, after the @moduledoc that ends at line 53); haiku-2, use GenServer only (line 49, after line 47); sonnet-1, use GenServer only (line 72, after line 70); sonnet-2, use GenServer only (line 57, after line 55). No run writes import, alias or require. Each use comes right after @moduledoc and a blank line, ahead of the module attributes. Violating runs: 0 of 4. Sonnet-1's example modules inside the moduledoc also open with their one use (use MyAppWeb, :controller at line 41, use Oban.Worker at line 60), and they have no @moduledoc. The case provokes only use, so the ordering part of the rule is never tested here.

The other nine rules are unchanged since 0397dec. git diff 0397dec -- idiomatic-elixir/ touches only the defstruct sentence under Update structs, the `do:` rule, the two new rules and testing.md. These nine are graded to the 2026-10-22-b standard: an `if` on one boolean condition is clean; an `if` inside a `case` goes under Keep functions short, not Branch (haiku-2 lines 153-158), as the previous two sweeps listed nested conditionals there; key, hit, entries, other and value are not counted under Naming; reading the limits file in init/1 is a missed case check but decides no verdict, because the responsive rule names only HTTP calls and large queries as slow work; Haiku-2's Jason compile warning appears in checks only, as in the previous sweep's skill-haiku-2. No run writes a `with`. Haiku-2 handles each single fallible call with a `case` (init/1 line 94, load_limits/1 lines 145-148, parse_limits/1 line 152), so it is clean, as opus-1's case on :file.consult/1 returning parse_limits/1 was in the previous sweep. Haiku-1, sonnet-1 and sonnet-2 load their limits with raising calls or matches at boot (File.read!/JSON.decode!, {:ok, [...]} = :file.consult(path), File.read!/String.to_integer), so they have no fallible tuple chain, and the with rule is not exercised in those three.

Designs: every run keeps one ETS row per admitted request in a public ordered_set table, owned by a GenServer that accepts :name. The caller inserts its row, counts with :ets.select_count/2 and deletes the row when over the limit, and a handle_info/2 sweep runs every 30 seconds (haiku-1, sonnet-2) or every minute (haiku-2, sonnet-1). Pick the abstraction, Use ETS, Keep each process behind one module, Supervise and the responsive rule are therefore clean in all four, as in the previous sweep. Haiku-1, haiku-2 and sonnet-2 keep the limits as rows in the same table, which the sweep's match spec leaves alone; sonnet-1 keeps them in :persistent_term. Every run reads the limits file in init/1: haiku-1 at line 101 (File.read! at line 137), haiku-2 at line 94 (File.read at line 145), sonnet-1 at line 113 (:file.consult at line 148), sonnet-2 at line 123 (File.read! at line 156). Sonnet-2 takes the default limit from the required :default_limit start option rather than from the file, as the previous sweep's sonnet-2 did.

Verification, in scratch copies under grading6/rate-limiter-skill. All four files pass mix format --check-formatted, and every session ran mix format itself. Haiku-1, sonnet-1 and sonnet-2 compile with elixirc --warnings-as-errors. Haiku-2 warns that Jason.decode/1 is undefined (line 152) because Jason is not installed; its session tested against a stub and left the call in, and with a stub over JSON.decode/1 it compiles and runs. In every run a 50-task burst admitted exactly 2 for a user at the default limit of 2 and 5 for a user configured at 5. A second instance started under name: :other kept its own count (2 of 50), and a sweep removed an injected 61-second-old row while keeping the live rows. Haiku-1 and haiku-2 compare user IDs with to_string/1, so 42 and "42" share a count and an override; sonnet-1 and sonnet-2 key by the raw ID, so "42" gets the default limit.

All four runs have rc 0 and a model_id matching their tier. Their skill_hash, 40c558766911fda74c71db955ccb8d004adbc77cf83dc8e44539667cc9de12c1, equals evals/tools/common.py folder_hash of the working tree's idiomatic-elixir/, so the runs saw the uncommitted text graded here.
